text_blocks.snippet: Spinal cord injury (SCI) levels refer to the location of the injury on the spinal cord, which dictates the extent of sensory and motor function loss below that point. The American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale categorizes SCI into five grades (A-E), with A being the most severe and E being the least.
snippet_highlighted_words: refer to the location of the injury on the spinal cord, which dictates the extent of sensory and motor function loss below that point

list.title: Grade A (Complete):
list.snippet: No sensory or motor function is preserved below the level of injury, including the anal area.

list.title: Grade B (Sensory Incomplete):
list.snippet: Sensory function is preserved below the injury level, but motor function is completely lost.

list.title: Grade C (Motor Incomplete):
list.snippet: Some motor function is preserved below the injury level, but less than half of the key muscles can be moved against gravity.

list.title: Grade D (Motor Incomplete):
list.snippet: More than half of the key muscles below the injury level can be moved against gravity.

list.title: Grade E (Normal):
list.snippet: Normal motor and sensory function has returned.

list.title: Neurological Level:
list.snippet: The neurological level of injury refers to the lowest point on the spinal cord where normal motor and sensory function is present.

list.title: Complete vs. Incomplete:
list.snippet: Complete injuries mean no function is preserved below the injury, while incomplete injuries indicate some function remains.

list.title: Location Matters:
list.snippet: Injuries higher on the spine (cervical region) typically result in more extensive paralysis (tetraplegia/quadriplegia) affecting all limbs, while injuries lower down (thoracic, lumbar, sacral regions) can cause paraplegia, affecting the lower body.

list.title: Cervical Injuries:
list.snippet: Injuries at the C1-C4 levels can result in tetraplegia, affecting the arms and legs.

list.title: Thoracic Injuries:
list.snippet: Injuries at the T1-T12 levels can result in paraplegia, affecting the lower body and potentially the trunk, depending on the specific level.

list.title: Lumbar and Sacral Injuries:
list.snippet: Injuries in these regions can affect the legs, hips, and bowel/bladder control, with varying degrees of severity.
